newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada merger activity up 22 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada merger activity up 22 pct in 1996.

text.p: Merger-hungry Canadian companies gobbled up 22 percent more acquisitions in 1996 than last year and the outlook is for more frenzied dealing in 1997, an industry group said on Wednesday.

"For 1997 we expect M & A activity levels to remain at historically high levels," Toronto-based Crosbie & Co Inc said in its 1996 report which included debt, cross-border deals and some mergers which have not closed yet.
Fueled by massive debt and equity financing available in a hot marketplace, Crosbie said it expects to see more partnerships and management buyouts in 1997.

"This increased MBO activity is directly related to the renewed availability of equity and sub-debt financing and the desire of many corporations to sell off their non-core operations," the agency said.
There were 1,184 mergers and acquisitions in the year, up 22 percent from 967 in 1995.
Despite the higher activity the value of these deals slipped to C$75.4 billion ($55.8 billion) in 1996 from C$77.4 billion ($57 billion) a year earlier, Crosbie said.

Crosbie's 1996 list included Houston-based Service Corp International's US$2.9 billion bid for Vancouver-based funeral home operator Loewen Group Inc is excluded. Service dropped its hostile bid for Loewen on Tuesday.
Activity in 1995 included C$20 billion ($15 billion) in transactions by Seagram Co Ltd selling its stake in DuPont Co and acquiring MCA Inc.
Crosbie said the five most active sectors based on transactions were industrial products, oil and gas, merchandising, consumer products, communications and media.
Oil and gas rang up the biggest value in 1996 with C$10.3 billion ($7.6 billion) on 148 deals, compared to 115 transactions in 1995 worth C$21 billion ($15.5 billion)

Activty in 1996 included Petro-Canada's acquisition of Amerada Hess Canada for C$735 million ($544 million). Crosbie also listed Gulf Canada Resources Ltd's C$972 million ($720 million) hostile bid for Britain's Clyde Petroleum Plc which is being opposed by Clyde.
The communications group posted the biggest transaction of the year -- Thomson's Corp's C$4.6 billion ($3.4 billion) takeover of West Publishing Co last February.
The second largest deal was nickel miner Inco Ltd's C$4.3 billion ($3.1 billion) purchase of Diamond Fields Resources Inc and its rich Newfoundland deposit.
Canadian gold producers were also major acquisitors in 1996. Peter Munk's Barrick Gold Corp grabbed junior minerals explorer Arequipa Resources Ltd for C$1.1 billion ($814 million).
Looking ahead to 1997, Barrick is poised to become the world's biggest gold producer if it acquires a majority stake in Bre-X Minerals Ltd's rich Indonesian gold find.

Crosbie said cross-border activity was up 22 percent in 1996 with Canadian firms unveiling 258 foreign deals worth C$21 billion ($15.5 billion). About 53 percent of their targets were in the United States.

Aside from Thomson Corp's acquisition of West Publishing, Toronto-Dominion Bank paid C$715 million ($529 million) for Waterhouse Investor Services Inc in a bid to become North America's biggest discount brokerage.

Foreign companies announced 150 Canadian acquisitions during 1996, up from 126 in the prior year. The leading country was again the United States with 122 transactions totalling C$14.3 billion ($10.5 billion), up 34 percent and 63 percent respectively from 1995.
The biggest U.S. purchase was Allied Waste Industries Inc's C$2.2 billion ($1.6 billion) acquisition of Laidlaw Inc's solid waste unit.

Laidlaw jumped back in the news on Monday with two major deals worth over US$2 billion, including the US$1.12 billion purchase of North America's leading ambulance operator, American Medical Response Inc.
